Kyanite is found in the schist of the Tallulah Falls formation; however, it is not sufficiently concentrated in the parent rock to warrant mining. Stream sand and gravel occur in the project area, but due to the dominance of silt and sand, excessive washing would be required before it could be used. Thus, potential for there being economic mineral deposits in the project is small.
Groundwater is found in joints, fractures, planes of cleavage, and schistosity of gneisses, schists, and granites in the Piedmont. Some rock types are more productive than others such as schistone rock types (Cazeau, 1967). Greater thicknesses of sapprolite have larger water storage capacity than a thin weathered blanket. Borings drilled in the reservoir rim at the Bad Creek Project had very erratic static water levels in the bore holes. In some borings the static water level was in bedrock and in other borings the water level was in the sapprolite with considerable variations in the water elevations in a short distance. Thus, the Applicant's statement that the classic concept of the water table cannot be applied to groundwater distribution and movement in the Blue Ridge and Piedmont appears to be verified by the borings. The water table appears to be a discontinuous surface. Potential seepage problems do exist in the thin reservoir rims which will be controlled by blanketing and drainage. Beyond this, the upper reservoir and project structures should have little appreciable impact on groundwater conditions.
2.1.4 <u>Soils</u>
The soils of the project area are residual, being derived from the in-situ weathering of the underlying bedrock. Generally, the soils tend to be granular with a high percentage of mica flakes as the main accessory mineral.
The surface soil or "A" horizon is thin and poorly developed. The organic content is low except in areas of dense vegetation. The underlying "B" horizon contains the highest percentage of clay-sized particles and varies from 0 to 5 feet in thickness.
The underlying "C" horizon is comprised of the deeply weathered and decomposed bedrock. This zone, commonly referred to as saprolite, is irregular in thickness and generally has a broad zone of gradational material at its base. The soil of this horizon is typically granular with mica flakes and irregular-sized blocks of the parent gneissic bedrock.
